title: RASteer: Retain-Aware Activation Steering for Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models

paper.title: RASteer: Retain-Aware Activation Steering for Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Concept erasure aims to remove a target concept, such as a copyrighted style, a recognizable character,
or unsafe content, from a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model while preserving its ability to generate
other content. Existing activation steering methods build an erasure direction mainly from the target
concept and adjust model activations along it at inference time. However, target and retained concepts
often overlap in the model’s representation space, so this direction also contains shared components that
retained concepts rely on. Steering directly along this direction can therefore suppress retained concepts
and harm the generation of non-target content. To address this issue, we propose R etain-aware A ctivation Steer ing ( RASteer ), a training-free method. RASteer first builds a retain subspace from the concepts to preserve.
Retain-Orthogonal Steering (ROS) then removes components aligned with this subspace from the erasure
direction, making steering more specific to the target. Since fully removing the shared components can
weaken erasure, we further introduce Overlap-Adaptive Calibration (OAC). At each layer and denoising step,
OAC uses the overlap between the erasure direction and the retain subspace to control how much of each
shared component is removed, balancing target erasure and concept preservation. Experiments on unsafe-content,
instance, and artistic-style erasure across multiple backbones and benchmarks show that RASteer matches or
outperforms the activation steering and weight editing baselines we evaluate, achieving a better
balance between erasure and preservation. 1 1 1 Project page: https://rasteer.cvmlgroup.web.illinois.edu/

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) are trained on web-scale data and inevitably learn content that their providers cannot include in their products, such as copyrighted artistic styles, recognizable characters, and unsafe images. When takedown requests, changes in regulations, or safety audits require removing such content, retraining on filtered data is too costly, while prompt- or output-level filters are easily bypassed ( Rando et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Sarwar et al., 2026 ) . Concept erasure offers a practical alternative: it directly edits a released model to prevent it from generating a target concept ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , and has become a key step in deploying T2I models responsibly. Such edits must erase the target while preserving all other content, including unrelated styles and characters, as well as open-domain generation. Existing erasure methods broadly fall into two categories: weight editing and activation steering. Weight editing fine-tunes the model or applies closed-form updates to its cross-attention matrices ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , writing these changes into model parameters and increasing the cost of switching or undoing edits. By contrast, activation steering ( Gaintseva et al., 2026 ; Huu-Tien et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ) keeps model weights fixed and suppresses target concepts by adjusting intermediate activations during inference, allowing edits to be enabled, disabled, or combined. The erasure direction is constructed from the target concept, and each image patch is gated based on its activation’s alignment with that direction. However, the target’s erasure direction may contain shared components that retained concepts also rely on, causing collateral damage. In the top row of Figure 1 a, steering along the original direction to erase Sonic turns the retained character Snoopy into an ordinary dog. Figure 1 b further shows overlap between the alignment scores of target and retained activations: at the default threshold, the gate incorrectly triggers on 65 % 65\% of retained activations and misses 21 % 21\% of target activations. Raising the threshold reduces false triggers but misses more target activations. In the bottom row of Figure 1 a, Snoopy remains recognizable after full projection even though it is the erasure target, showing that completely removing shared components can also weaken target erasure. These observations show the need to incorporate information about retained concepts into the erasure direction to reduce collateral damage and improve target erasure. Figure 1: Erasure–preservation trade-offs in steering. (a) Collateral damage from original-direction steering (top) and incomplete erasure under full projection (bottom). (b) Fractions of activations above each threshold. (c) Target and mean retained CLIP accuracy for Snoopy erasure. To address these issues, we propose R etain-aware A ctivation Steer ing ( RASteer ), which uses information about retained concepts to refine the erasure direction. It consists of two modules: Retain-Orthogonal Steering (ROS) and Overlap-Adaptive Calibration (OAC). ROS constructs a retain subspace from the steering vectors of retained concepts. It identifies and reduces the shared components of the original erasure direction that align with this subspace, making the direction more specific to the target and reducing suppression of retained concepts. OAC adjusts the removal strength based on the overlap between the erasure direction and the retain subspace at each layer and denoising step, balancing target erasure and concept preservation. As shown in Figure 1 c, RASteer further lowers target classification accuracy compared with full projection while maintaining similar accuracy on retained concepts, illustrating how adaptive calibration improves target erasure. We evaluate RASteer on unsafe-content, instance, and artistic-style erasure across multiple backbones and benchmarks, comparing against activation-steering and weight-editing baselines under the same evaluation pipeline. The results show that RASteer effectively suppresses target concepts while largely preserving retained concepts and general image quality, achieving a better trade-off between erasure and preservation. Our contributions are: • We propose RASteer , a closed-form, training-free method that erases concepts by steering cross-attention activations while keeping model weights fixed and edits reversible and composable. • We introduce ROS to remove retain-subspace components from erasure directions and OAC to adjust removal strength at each layer based on erasure–retain overlap, without learnable parameters. • Across unsafe-content, instance, and artistic-style erasure on multiple backbones and benchmarks, RASteer achieves the best erasure–preservation trade-off among the compared methods.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Model Editing for Concept Erasure. Fine-tuning methods suppress concepts by optimizing the denoiser ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) or training lightweight modules ( Lyu et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . Closed-form methods directly update cross-attention weights: TIME ( Orgad et al., 2023 ) uses least-squares editing, UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) adds retention constraints, and RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) iteratively erases embeddings that regenerate the target. MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) combines closed-form editing with LoRA fusion for mass erasure Hu et al. (2021) . SPEED ( Li et al., 2026 ) restricts updates to the null space of preserved concepts, while CURE ( Biswas et al., 2026 ) applies an energy-scaled spectral projection. These methods encode edits in model weights or trained modules, so switching or combining edits involves managing the corresponding parameters. Inference-Time Steering. The most recent family leaves the weights untouched and edits the generation process at inference: Safe Latent Diffusion ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) steers the sampling trajectory away from unsafe content through classifier-free guidance, SAFREE ( Yoon et al., 2025 ) projects prompt embeddings off the unsafe concept’s subspace in text-embedding space, SAeUron ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) ablates sparse-autoencoder features of the target, and CASteer ( Gaintseva et al., 2026 ) subtracts the target’s steering vector from cross-attention activations, keeping the edit reversible and composable. All of them, however, model only the concept to remove : none takes the concepts to keep as input, so a retained concept that shares directions with the target is suppressed along with it. RASteer keeps this weight-free runtime and supplies the missing ingredient: it builds a retain subspace from the concepts to preserve and steers only along the erasure direction orthogonal to it, with layerwise strength set by overlap. Sequential and Continual Unlearning. Continual learning studies how models acquire a sequence of tasks or concepts while mitigating interference with previously learned knowledge, whereas online learning emphasizes adaptation to a stream of incoming data or objectives Liu et al. (2020) ; Liu et al. (2021a) ; Liu et al. (2021b) ; Liu et al. (2023a) ; Liu et al. (2023b) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2019) ; Li et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Fischer et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2023) . Sequential unlearning presents a complementary challenge: rather than continually acquiring new knowledge, a deployed model must continually satisfy new forgetting requests while retaining everything else Meng et al. (2022a) ; Meng et al. (2022b) ; Ma et al. (2025) ; Gu et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2024) . Repeated parameter editing can accumulate interference across requests, making preservation increasingly difficult. Our setting shares this continual adaptation perspective, but differs in that RASteer performs each edit at inference time without updating model parameters, allowing multiple erasure constraints to be introduced, removed, or combined without parameter drift.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Section 3.1 formalizes the concept-erasure setting and shows how we extract a steering direction for a concept. Section 3.2 then presents RASteer and its two modules: Retain-Orthogonal Steering (ROS), which applies this direction after projecting out its retain-aligned part, and Overlap-Adaptive Calibration (OAC), which sets the projection strength directly from data.

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries
sections.text: Let 𝒰 \mathcal{U} be the set of concepts the text encoder of a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model can represent. We seek to suppress concepts in an erasure set ℱ ⊆ 𝒰 \mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{U} while preserving those in a retain set ℛ ⊆ 𝒰 \mathcal{R}\subseteq\mathcal{U} . Given a prompt p p , let 𝐜 ∈ ℝ d \mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the output activation at one image patch of a cross-attention layer in the denoising U-Net. At each layer and denoising step, we obtain a concept direction by normalizing the difference between mean activations for paired prompts with and without the concept. CASteer ( Gaintseva et al., 2026 ) uses the target direction 𝐟 ^ \hat{\mathbf{f}} to update 𝐜 \mathbf{c} during inference as: 𝐜 ′ = 𝐜 − β ​ g ​ ( 𝐜 ) ​ 𝐟 ^ , g ⁡ ( 𝐜 ) = max ⁡ ( ⟨ 𝐟 ^ , 𝐜 ⟩ , 0 ) , \mathbf{c}^{\prime}=\mathbf{c}-\beta\,g(\mathbf{c})\,\hat{\mathbf{f}},\qquad g(\mathbf{c})=\max\!\big(\langle\hat{\mathbf{f}},\mathbf{c}\rangle,\,0\big), (1) where β \beta controls steering strength. sections.heading: 4.1 Setup
sections.text: Backbones and Benchmarks. We use Stable Diffusion v1.4 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) as the main backbone and evaluate cross-model generality on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and v2.1, plus SDXL ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) . We evaluate unsafe content on I2P prompts ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) , instances and artistic styles with matched retain concepts, and general open-domain generation on MS-COCO captions ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . We compare with SPM ( Lyu et al., 2024 ) , SAeUron ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) , ESD-x/u ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) , MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) , and CASteer ( Gaintseva et al., 2026 ) . Implementation Details. RASteer is training-free and updates no weights. For each concept, we precompute its steering vectors offline and reuse them at inference. We steer every cross-attention layer with the OAC rule and no per-concept tuning. We use official code or released weights under default settings for every baseline. Experiments use NVIDIA A40. Appendix A.1 provides the complete implementation details. Evaluation Metrics. We measure erasure and preservation jointly. Concept presence is scored by CLIP accuracy and CLIP score ( Radford et al., 2021 ) on the erasure target and on every retained concept. Unsafe content is counted by the exposed body parts detected with NudeNet ( Bedapudi, 2019 ) . On COCO, CLIP score measures image–caption alignment, while FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) measure distribution-level and paired-image drift from the unsteered backbone’s generations under the same prompts and seeds. For instance and style experiments, FID is computed against the corresponding unsteered concept generations.

sections.heading: 4.3 Ablation Study
sections.text: Component Ablation. Table 4 uses the first block of Table 3 , erasing Snoopy and Van Gogh while treating the other concepts in their respective groups as retained concepts. All variants use the same vector configuration. Removing ROS recovers raw activation steering. Its retained-concept FID increases consistently, accompanied by lower recognition accuracy for several retained concepts, showing that ROS is responsible for limiting collateral changes. Removing OAC instead applies the full retain projection at every layer and step. For both erased concepts, this variant has higher target CLIP score and lower target FID, indicating that its outputs remain closer to the original target semantics and distribution. Van Gogh accuracy is an exception to this trend, so we interpret the erasure effect jointly through alignment and distributional change rather than accuracy alone. Together, the two ablations suggest complementary roles: ROS protects retained concepts, while OAC prevents the retain projection from removing too much of the target-specific erasure direction. Cross-Attention Layer Scope. We compare five steering scopes with other settings fixed. Figure 5 a shows that Middle and High leave target CLIP accuracy above 96%, whereas Low reduces it to 10.8% for the instance and 35.8% for the style. Low+Mid matches All in target accuracy at 10.8% and 32.9%, respectively. Figure 5 b shows retained-concept accuracy above 98% across all scopes. However, Figure 5 c reveals lower retained FID for Low+Mid than All: 61.7 versus 70.8 for the instance and 83.9 versus 86.5 for the style. Thus, extending Low+Mid to All increases distributional drift without further reducing target accuracy in this comparison. We retain All as the default across backbones to avoid selecting a separate layer mask for each architecture. Steering Strength. We vary β \beta from 1.5 to 4 using the evaluation protocols in Sec. 4.1 . Figure 5 a shows that target CLIP accuracy falls from 29.5% to 7.9% for instances and from 38.2% to 1.7% for styles. I2P detections, however, reach a minimum of 4 at β = 3 \beta=3 before rising to 16 at β = 4 \beta=4 . Figure 5 b shows retained-concept accuracy declining from 99.3% to 98.1% for instances and from 99.0% to 93.3% for styles, while COCO LPIPS increases. Retained-concept and COCO FID also increase throughout the sweep in Figure 5 c. Stronger steering therefore improves instance and style erasure at the cost of greater changes to retained and general content, without consistently improving unsafe-content removal. The default β = 2 \beta=2 on SD-v1.4 keeps retained-concept accuracy above 98% while limiting drift relative to larger strengths.

sections.heading: 4.4 Qualitative Results
sections.text: Figure 6 compares Snoopy erasure (top) and Mickey retention (bottom) on SD-v2.1. RASteer removes Snoopy from the first scene; face-like remnants and texture artifacts persist in the other erased rows. SAeUron retains target cues, while ESD and RECE also distort retained images. Compared with CASteer, RASteer better preserves Mickey’s facial structure and the origami layout, showing improved preservation despite residual erasure artifacts. Appendix A.3 provides additional visualizations for style and cross-backbone comparisons.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied concept erasure through inference-time activation steering, where the target concept may share substantial representation with concepts that should be retained. We traced the collateral damage of raw steering to this overlap and proposed RASteer, a training-free method that leaves the model weights unchanged. Its ROS module removes retain-aligned components from the erasure direction, while OAC adjusts the removal strength according to the target–retain overlap. Across multiple concept-erasure benchmarks and four Stable Diffusion backbones, RASteer balances target suppression with preservation of retained concepts and general generation. Limitations. First, our experiments focus on the Stable Diffusion family; extending RASteer to newer architectures such as diffusion transformers and FLUX remains future work. Second, RASteer relies on a predefined retain set, and poorly represented concepts may still be affected. Third, when the target direction overlaps substantially with the retain subspace, the direction available for erasure becomes limited, motivating adaptive retain-set construction or iterative steering.

sections.heading: A.1 Additional Implementation Details
sections.text: We use Stable Diffusion v1.4 as the main backbone and evaluate transfer on Stable Diffusion v1.5, Stable Diffusion v2.1, and SDXL. All models run in half precision with their released pipeline defaults. The SD-v1.4, SD-v1.5, and SD-v2.1 experiments use 50 denoising steps; SDXL uses 30. The steering strength is fixed per backbone and never tuned per concept: β = 2 \beta=2 for SD-v1.4 and SD-v1.5, and β = 3 \beta=3 for SD-v2.1 and SDXL. We apply the clipping rule in Eq. 1 at every denoising step. Figure 5 reports the sensitivity to β \beta on SD-v1.4.

sections.heading: A.3 Additional Qualitative Comparisons
sections.text: Figures 7 – 10 extend the main-text comparison to all four backbones. Every figure uses the same layout: three erased instances, three retained instances, three erased styles, and three retained styles. Columns show the unedited backbone, each supported baseline, and RASteer. Within a row, all methods use the same prompt and seed; differences can therefore be read as method effects rather than prompt or sampling variation. We analyze each row from left to right along two axes. For an erased row, success requires both removal of the target identity or style and a visually coherent replacement; a recognizable Snoopy or Van Gogh signature indicates under-erasure, whereas repeated textures, collapsed structure, or an empty scene indicate over-erasure. For a retained row, we compare identity, composition, color, and texture against the unedited output in the first column. Large deviations reveal collateral damage even when the erased target itself is absent. Across SD-v1.4 and SD-v1.5, RASteer generally removes the target while producing structured alternatives, whereas several baselines either retain recognizable target cues or alter nearby concepts. SD-v2.1 is the more difficult regime: residual target cues occur more often, but the retained Mickey Mouse and Hokusai rows remain comparatively stable under RASteer. On SDXL, target removal is strong and the retained Pikachu and artistic-style rows expose the preservation advantage most clearly; the remaining texture changes in erased-style rows also show that strong erasure is not artifact-free. These recurring patterns match the quantitative erasure–preservation trade-off rather than relying on a single favorable sample. A backbone-specific reading further separates the failure modes. On SD-v1.4 and SD-v1.5, incomplete instance erasure often leaves a recognizable silhouette, while stronger interventions can replace the entire subject or background. In the style rows, some methods suppress the named painter by flattening the image into repetitive texture rather than preserving the prompt content. SD-v2.1 shows the same effects more strongly: residual character shapes and dense repeated motifs coexist across methods. The SDXL rows make collateral damage especially easy to see because its unedited outputs are highly consistent; the retained Pikachu poses and wave-like compositions stay close under RASteer, whereas some baselines alter the subject, palette, or spatial structure. Thus the grid distinguishes successful semantic removal from mere visual degradation. Figure 7: Additional instance and style comparisons on Stable Diffusion v1.4. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.01969v1 [cs.CV] 01 Oct 2026 RASteer: Retain-Aware Activation Steering for Concept Erasure in Diffusion Models Yongliang Wu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Haori Lu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Yulun Wu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Jinqi Luo Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania Xingyu Zhu † † thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: National University of Singapore Yaoyao Liu Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Abstract Concept erasure aims to remove a target concept, such as a copyrighted style, a recognizable character, or unsafe content, from a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model while preserving its ability to generate other content. Existing activation steering methods build an erasure direction mainly from the target concept and adjust model activations along it at inference time. However, target and retained concepts often overlap in the model’s representation space, so this direction also contains shared components that retained concepts rely on. Steering directly along this direction can therefore suppress retained concepts and harm the generation of non-target content. To address this issue, we propose R etain-aware A ctivation Steer ing ( RASteer ), a training-free method. RASteer first builds a retain subspace from the concepts to preserve. Retain-Orthogonal Steering (ROS) then removes components aligned with this subspace from the erasure direction, making steering more specific to the target. Since fully removing the shared components can weaken erasure, we further introduce Overlap-Adaptive Calibration (OAC). At each layer and denoising step, OAC uses the overlap between the erasure direction and the retain subspace to control how much of each shared component is removed, balancing target erasure and concept preservation. Experiments on unsafe-content, instance, and artistic-style erasure across multiple backbones and benchmarks show that RASteer matches or outperforms the activation steering and weight editing baselines we evaluate, achieving a better balance between erasure and preservation. 1 1 1 Project page: https://rasteer.cvmlgroup.web.illinois.edu/ 1 Introduction Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) are trained on web-scale data and inevitably learn content that their providers cannot include in their products, such as copyrighted artistic styles, recognizable characters, and unsafe images. When takedown requests, changes in regulations, or safety audits require removing such content, retraining on filtered data is too costly, while prompt- or output-level filters are easily bypassed ( Rando et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Sarwar et al., 2026 ) . Concept erasure offers a practical alternative: it directly edits a released model to prevent it from generating a target concept ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , and has become a key step in deploying T2I models responsibly. Such edits must erase the target while preserving all other content, including unrelated styles and characters, as well as open-domain generation. Existing erasure methods broadly fall into two categories: weight editing and activation steering. Weight editing fine-tunes the model or applies closed-form updates to its cross-attention matrices ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Gandikota et al., 2024 ; Gong et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , writing these changes into model parameters and increasing the cost of switching or undoing edits. By contrast, activation steering ( Gaintseva et al., 2026 ; Huu-Tien et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2024b ) keeps model weights fixed and suppresses target concepts by adjusting intermediate activations during inference, allowing edits to be enabled, disabled, or combined. The erasure direction is constructed from the target concept, and each image patch is gated based on its activation’s alignment with that direction. However, the target’s erasure direction may contain shared components that retained concepts also rely on, causing collateral damage. In the top row of Figure 1 a, steering along the original direction to erase Sonic turns the retained character Snoopy into an ordinary dog. Figure 1 b further shows overlap between the alignment scores of target and retained activations: at the default threshold, the gate incorrectly triggers on 65 % 65\% of retained activations and misses 21 % 21\% of target activations. Raising the threshold reduces false triggers but misses more target activations. In the bottom row of Figure 1 a, Snoopy remains recognizable after full projection even though it is the erasure target, showing that completely removing shared components can also weaken target erasure. These observations show the need to incorporate information about retained concepts into the erasure direction to reduce collateral damage and improve target erasure. (b) Fractions of activations above each threshold. (c) Target and mean retained CLIP accuracy for Snoopy erasure. To address these issues, we propose R etain-aware A ctivation Steer ing ( RASteer ), which uses information about retained concepts to refine the erasure direction. It consists of two modules: Retain-Orthogonal Steering (ROS) and Overlap-Adaptive Calibration (OAC). ROS constructs a retain subspace from the steering vectors of retained concepts. It identifies and reduces the shared components of the original erasure direction that align with this subspace, making the direction more specific to the target and reducing suppression of retained concepts. OAC adjusts the removal strength based on the overlap between the erasure direction and the retain subspace at each layer and denoising step, balancing target erasure and concept preservation. As shown in Figure 1 c, RASteer further lowers target classification accuracy compared with full projection while maintaining similar accuracy on retained concepts, illustrating how adaptive calibration improves target erasure. We evaluate RASteer on unsafe-content, instance, and artistic-style erasure across multiple backbones and benchmarks, comparing against activation-steering and weight-editing baselines under the same evaluation pipeline. The results show that RASteer effectively suppresses target concepts while largely preserving retained concepts and general image quality, achieving a better trade-off between erasure and preservation. Our contributions are: • We propose RASteer , a closed-form, training-free method that erases concepts by steering cross-attention activations while keeping model weights fixed and edits reversible and composable. • We introduce ROS to remove retain-subspace components from erasure directions and OAC to adjust removal strength at each layer based on erasure–retain overlap, without learnable parameters. • Across unsafe-content, instance, and artistic-style erasure on multiple backbones and benchmarks, RASteer achieves the best erasure–preservation trade-off among the compared methods. 2 Related Work Model Editing for Concept Erasure. Fine-tuning methods suppress concepts by optimizing the denoiser ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ; Kumari et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) or training lightweight modules ( Lyu et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . Closed-form methods directly update cross-attention weights: TIME ( Orgad et al., 2023 ) uses least-squares editing, UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) adds retention constraints, and RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) iteratively erases embeddings that regenerate the target. MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) combines closed-form editing with LoRA fusion for mass erasure Hu et al. (2021) . SPEED ( Li et al., 2026 ) restricts updates to the null space of preserved concepts, while CURE ( Biswas et al., 2026 ) applies an energy-scaled spectral projection. These methods encode edits in model weights or trained modules, so switching or combining edits involves managing the corresponding parameters. Inference-Time Steering. The most recent family leaves the weights untouched and edits the generation process at inference: Safe Latent Diffusion ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) steers the sampling trajectory away from unsafe content through classifier-free guidance, SAFREE ( Yoon et al., 2025 ) projects prompt embeddings off the unsafe concept’s subspace in text-embedding space, SAeUron ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) ablates sparse-autoencoder features of the target, and CASteer ( Gaintseva et al., 2026 ) subtracts the target’s steering vector from cross-attention activations, keeping the edit reversible and composable. All of them, however, model only the concept to remove : none takes the concepts to keep as input, so a retained concept that shares directions with the target is suppressed along with it. RASteer keeps this weight-free runtime and supplies the missing ingredient: it builds a retain subspace from the concepts to preserve and steers only along the erasure direction orthogonal to it, with layerwise strength set by overlap. Sequential and Continual Unlearning. Continual learning studies how models acquire a sequence of tasks or concepts while mitigating interference with previously learned knowledge, whereas online learning emphasizes adaptation to a stream of incoming data or objectives Liu et al. (2020) ; Liu et al. (2021a) ; Liu et al. (2021b) ; Liu et al. (2023a) ; Liu et al. (2023b) ; Liu et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2019) ; Li et al. (2020) ; Li et al. (2021) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Fischer et al. (2024) ; Zhang et al. (2023) . Sequential unlearning presents a complementary challenge: rather than continually acquiring new knowledge, a deployed model must continually satisfy new forgetting requests while retaining everything else Meng et al. (2022a) ; Meng et al. (2022b) ; Ma et al. (2025) ; Gu et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2024) . Repeated parameter editing can accumulate interference across requests, making preservation increasingly difficult. Our setting shares this continual adaptation perspective, but differs in that RASteer performs each edit at inference time without updating model parameters, allowing multiple erasure constraints to be introduced, removed, or combined without parameter drift. 3 Method Section 3.1 formalizes the concept-erasure setting and shows how we extract a steering direction for a concept. We use Stable Diffusion v1.4 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) as the main backbone and evaluate cross-model generality on Stable Diffusion v1.5 and v2.1, plus SDXL ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) . We evaluate unsafe content on I2P prompts ( Schramowski et al., 2023 ) , instances and artistic styles with matched retain concepts, and general open-domain generation on MS-COCO captions ( Lin et al., 2014 ) . We compare with SPM ( Lyu et al., 2024 ) , SAeUron ( Cywiński and Deja, 2025 ) , ESD-x/u ( Gandikota et al., 2023 ) , UCE ( Gandikota et al., 2024 ) , MACE ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , RECE ( Gong et al., 2024 ) , and CASteer ( Gaintseva et al., 2026 ) . Implementation Details. RASteer is training-free and updates no weights. For each concept, we precompute its steering vectors offline and reuse them at inference. We steer every cross-attention layer with the OAC rule and no per-concept tuning. We use official code or released weights under default settings for every baseline. Experiments use NVIDIA A40. Appendix A.1 provides the complete implementation details. Evaluation Metrics. We measure erasure and preservation jointly. Concept presence is scored by CLIP accuracy and CLIP score ( Radford et al., 2021 ) on the erasure target and on every retained concept. Unsafe content is counted by the exposed body parts detected with NudeNet ( Bedapudi, 2019 ) . On COCO, CLIP score measures image–caption alignment, while FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) measure distribution-level and paired-image drift from the unsteered backbone’s generations under the same prompts and seeds. For instance and style experiments, FID is computed against the corresponding unsteered concept generations. 4.2 Main Results We compare RASteer with all baselines on unsafe-content, instance, and artistic-style erasure. Appendix A.3 provides additional visualizations for style and cross-backbone comparisons. 5 Conclusion We studied concept erasure through inference-time activation steering, where the target concept may share substantial representation with concepts that should be retained. We traced the collateral damage of raw steering to this overlap and proposed RASteer, a training-free method that leaves the model weights unchanged. Its ROS module removes retain-aligned components from the erasure direction, while OAC adjusts the removal strength according to the target–retain overlap. Across multiple concept-erasure benchmarks and four Stable Diffusion backbones, RASteer balances target suppression with preservation of retained concepts and general generation. Limitations. First, our experiments focus on the Stable Diffusion family; extending RASteer to newer architectures such as diffusion transformers and FLUX remains future work. Second, RASteer relies on a predefined retain set, and poorly represented concepts may still be affected. Third, when the target direction overlaps substantially with the retain subspace, the direction available for erasure becomes limited, motivating adaptive retain-set construction or iterative steering.
